# Example workflow

## Example workflow

Continuing with the `penguins` dataset, we'll cover:

- Summaries and tables
- Data visualisation
- Regression

# Summaries and tables

## `dplyr::summarise()` 

The `summarise()` function applies the specified summary to the whole dataset

:::{.fragment}
```{r}
#| output-location: column
data |> 
  summarise(
    number_penguins = n(),
    mean_body_mass = mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = c(species, sex)
  )
```
:::

::: {.incremental}
- If `.by` is specified, it applies the summaries within each group
- The summary is returned in the same format as the input (data frame, tibble) 

:::

## `janitor::tabyl()` 

The `tabyl()` function is a convenient way to tabulate data.

:::{.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out}
One variable

```{r}
#| output-location: column
library(janitor)
data |> 
  tabyl(species)
```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out}
Two variables

```{r}
#| output-location: column
data |> 
  tabyl(species, sex)
```
:::

::: {.incremental}
- When tabulating two variables, the first argument is for rows, the second argument is for columns
- In both cases, the tabulation is returned as a data frame

:::

## `janitor::tabyl()` 

There are several helper functions starting with `adorn_*`, that add to the tabulation

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out}
```{r}
#| output-location: column
data |> 
  tabyl(species) |> 
  adorn_pct_formatting()
```
:::
::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-semi-out}
For two variables, `adorn_*` functions sometimes need rows or columns specified

```{r}
#| output-location: column
data |> 
  tabyl(species, sex) |> 
  adorn_totals("col") |> 
  adorn_percentages("row") |> 
  adorn_ns()
```
:::

## `gtsummary`

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
The `gtsummary` package has many functions for producing summary tables

```{r}
library(gtsummary)
```

We'll focus on the `tbl_summary()` function
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
# Function arguments
tbl_summary(
  data,
  by = NULL,
  label = NULL,
  statistic = list(all_continuous() ~ "{median} ({p25}, {p75})", all_categorical() ~
    "{n} ({p}%)"),
  digits = NULL,
  type = NULL,
  value = NULL,
  missing = c("ifany", "no", "always"),
  missing_text = "Unknown",
  missing_stat = "{N_miss}",
  sort = all_categorical(FALSE) ~ "alphanumeric",
  percent = c("column", "row", "cell"),
  include = everything()
)
```
:::
::::

## `tbl_summary()`

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
```{r}
penguin_summary <- tbl_summary(
  data,
  by = species,    # <1>
  include = c(     # <2>
    sex,           # <2>
    bill_len,      # <2>
    flipper_len,   # <2>
  )                # <2>
)
```

1. Which variable to produce summaries by
2. Which variables to summarise

:::
::: {.column}
```{r}
#| echo: false
library(gt)
penguin_summary |> 
  as_gt() |> 
  tab_options(
    table.width = pct(100),
    table.font.size = px(30),
    table.margin.left = px(10)
  )
```

:::
::::

## `tbl_summary()`

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

To save the output from `tbl_summary()`, we:

- convert it to a `tibble`
- save this as `csv` file

```{r}
penguin_summary |> 
  as_tibble() |> 
  write_csv(
    "data/penguin_summary.csv",
    na = ""
    )
```

## Other packages for tables

Creating tables via Quarto or RMarkdown:

- `flextable` has the best MS Word support
- `kable` is good for PDF output
- `gt` is highly customisable for HTML output

These do not create summaries for you!

```{r}
)
```

# Data visualisation

## Package options

`plot()` — base R

`ggplot2` — part of the `tidyverse`, highly customisable

`tidyplots` — simpler interface to `ggplot2`

## `ggplot2`

There are many plot types available, including:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

Raw data

- Scatter plots (`geom_point()`)
- Dot plots (`geom_dotplot()`)
- Line graph (`geom_line()`)

Summaries

- Bar plots (`geom_bar()`, `geom_col()`)
- Bars with errors (`geom_errorbar()`)
- Box and whisker plots (`geom_boxplot()`)

:::
::: {.column}

Distributions

- Histogram (`geom_hist()`)
- Density (`geom_density()`)
- Violin (`geom_violin()`)

:::
::::
::: {.callout-tip}
See the documentation for all available plots <https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/index.html>
:::

## `ggplot2`

All plots start with the `ggplot()` function

```{r}
#| output-location: column
ggplot(
  data,
  aes(
    x = flipper_len,
    y = bill_len
  )
)
```

## Scatter plot

From this, we add to the plot using the `+` symbol

```{r}
#| output-location: column
ggplot(
  data,
  aes(
    x = flipper_len,
    y = bill_len
  )
) +
  geom_point()
```

## Bar plot

For some plots, it doesn't make sense to plot the raw data.

```{r}
#| output-location: column
ggplot(
  data,
  aes(
    x = species,
    y = body_mass
  )
) +
  geom_col()
```

::: {.callout-tip}
Use `geom_col()` on summarised data, `geom_bar()` to summarise raw data
:::

## Bar plot

Instead, we need to summarise the data first and plot the summarised values

```{r}
#| output-location: column
data |> 
  summarise(
    mean_body_mass = mean(body_mass, na.rm = T),
    .by = species
  ) |> 
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = species,
      y = mean_body_mass
    )
  ) +
  geom_col()
```

::: {.callout-tip}
Use `geom_col()` on summarised data, `geom_bar()` to summarise raw data
:::

## Line graph

```{r}
#| output-location: column
ggplot(
  data,
  aes(
    x = year,
    y = body_mass
  )
) +
geom_line()
```

## Line graph

```{r}
#| output-location: column
data |>
  summarise(
    mean_body_mass = mean(body_mass, na.rm = T),
    .by = c(year, species)
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = year,
      y = mean_body_mass,
      colour = species
    )
  ) +
  geom_line()
```

# Questions?

## Customising a plot

```{r}
#| output-location: column
penguin_plot <- ggplot(
  data,
  aes(
    x = flipper_len,
    y = bill_len,
    colour = species
  )
) +
  geom_point(
    size = 3,
    shape = 1
    )

penguin_plot
```

## Customising axes

```{r}
#| output-location: column
penguin_plot <- penguin_plot +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "Flipper length (mm)",
    limits = c(160, 240),
    breaks = seq(160,240,20),
    minor_breaks = NULL
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Bill length (mm)",
    limits = c(30, 60),
    breaks = seq(30, 60, 10),
    minor_breaks = seq(35, 55, 10)
  ) 
penguin_plot
```

## Customising the legend

```{r}
#| output-location: column
penguin_plot <- penguin_plot + 
  scale_colour_manual(
    name = "Species",
    values = c("#1b9e77", "#d95f02", "#7570b3")
  ) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 6)))
penguin_plot
```

## Customising with a theme

```{r}
#| output-location: column
penguin_plot <- penguin_plot + 
  theme_bw(
    base_size = 25,
    base_family = "serif"
  )
penguin_plot
```

::: {.callout-tip}
There are several themes available! `theme_minimal()` is popular, but has a transparent background.
:::

## Adding an element

```{r}
#| output-location: column
penguin_plot <- penguin_plot +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    linetype = "dashed",
    show.legend = FALSE
  )
penguin_plot
```

## Adding a facet

```{r}
#| output-location: column
penguin_plot <- penguin_plot +
  facet_wrap(~ sex)
penguin_plot
```

## Saving the output

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

```{r}
ggsave(
  "img/penguin_plot.png",
  penguin_plot,
  width = 16,
  height = 9,
  units = "in",
)
```

## Let's practice!

::::: {.columns}
:::: {.column width="65%"}

Use `ggplot2` to make a bar chart showing the count of each penguin species, format the axes, and add a theme.

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Initial specification"
practice_plot <- ggplot(
  data,
  aes(
    x = species
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Adding the bars"
practice_plot <- practice_plot +
  geom_bar()
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Format the axes"
practice_plot <- practice_plot +
  scale_x_discrete(
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Count",
    limits = c(0, 160)
  )
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Add a theme"
practice_plot <- practice_plot +
  theme_bw()
```

# Regression

## Model notation

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
To regress `body_mass` on `sex` and `species`, we write:

```{r}
regression_results <- lm(
  body_mass ~ sex + species,
  data = data
)
```

Outcome (`body_mass`) left of the tilde `~`

Covariates right of the tilde, separated with a plus `+`

:::
::: {.column width="40%" .fragment}

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Function arguments
lm(
  formula, 
  data, 
  subset, 
  weights, 
  na.action,
  method = "qr",
  model = TRUE, 
  x = FALSE, 
  y = FALSE, 
  qr = TRUE,
  singular.ok = TRUE,
  contrasts = NULL,
  offset, 
  ...,
  digits
  )
```

:::
::::



<!-- ## Interaction temrs -->

<!-- Interaction terms can be specified  -->

<!-- `mpg ~ hp + cyl*disp` -->

<!-- or -->

<!-- `mpg ~ hp + cyl:disp` -->

## Model fit

You can plot the output of `lm()`

```{r}
#| output-location: column
plot(regression_results)
```

## Accessing model results

`gtsummary` has a function for this ^[I only found this out while making this workshop]

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
```{r}
#| eval: false
tbl_regression(
  regression_results,
  intercept = TRUE,
  pvalue_fun = label_style_pvalue(digits = 3)
  )
```
:::
::: {.column}
```{r}
#| echo: false
tbl_regression(
  regression_results,
  intercept = TRUE,
  pvalue_fun = label_style_pvalue(digits = 3)
  ) |> 
  as_gt() |> 
  tab_options(
    table.width = pct(100),
    table.font.size = px(30),
    table.margin.left = px(10)
  )
```
:::
::::

## Available models*

Base R:

- Linear `lm()`
- Generalised linear `glm()`
- Time series `ar()`, `arima()`, `arima0()`

Packages for common models:

- `survival` for survival analysis
- `gee` for generalised estimating equations
- `lme4` and `glmmTMB` for mixed-effects models
- `brms` Bayesian stuff
- `gam` and `gamlss` for generalised additive models
